paper.title: On The Harmonic Index and The Girth for Graphs
paper.abstract: Determines the minimum and maximum values of the harmonic index (sum over edges of 2/(d(u)+d(v))) for connected graphs with girth at least k (k >= 3), characterises the extremal graphs, and derives several relations between the harmonic index and the girth.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

flag_details.NO_LIMITATIONS: No limitations section and no inline acknowledgment of constraints or open questions; the paper ends with the last proof and the acknowledgements.

verdict.summary: Short extremal graph theory paper with proportionate, necessary formalism; moderate self-citation on the same topic; no limitations stated.

papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Extremal bounds on the harmonic index of connected graphs with a girth constraint, plus derived relations between index and girth.
**Level:** 3 (Medium)
**Rationale:** Proves new, non-trivial extremal results with characterisation of extremal graphs (induction on m+n with case analysis). It is not a complexity, protocol or verification result, so Level 4 is not warranted.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 numbered (standard graph notation introduced inline)
- Theorems: 7 (Lemmas 2.1-2.3 cited from prior work, Theorems 2.4-2.7)
- Proofs: 2 (Theorem 2.4 and Theorem 2.7; 2.5 and 2.6 follow directly)
- Equations: about 15 display equations, all part of the proofs

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 29
Expected range (Level 3): 10-40
Ratio: 0.73x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. Every formal element is the subject matter; the bounds cannot be stated or proved in plain English.

### Issues
None identified. The Theorem 2.4 proof is careful (pendent-vertex case, cut-edge and non-cut-edge subcases). The Subcase 2.1 bound relies on n_i >= k; the numerical step is terse but checkable.

---

## Citation Analysis

25 references, 4 by the author ([19], [20], [21], [22], the last a preprint), SCR 16%. All four concern the harmonic index of related graph classes and are directly used (Lemma 2.3 comes from [19]); relevance is high. The ratio falls in the 15-20% elevated band but has no padding pattern.

---

## Structural Analysis

Claims are mathematical and backed by proofs. The paper has no conclusion, no discussion of open problems and no limitations. Nothing to release as an artifact (pure theory).

---

## Conclusion

A competent, narrowly scoped extremal graph theory note whose formalism is exactly what the results require. Its only weaknesses are structural: it says nothing about scope or open questions, and it leans moderately on the author's own earlier harmonic-index results, though these are pertinent.

paper.title: Nominal Techniques for πI-Calculus
paper.abstract: Presents a nominal semantics for the πI-calculus whose transition rules are written compactly in nominal logic using the universal and nominal (N) quantifiers, and proves that this semantics is equivalent to Sangiorgi's original semantics of the πI-calculus.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

flag_details.ELEVATED_FORMALISM: Formalism complexity 101 (16 definitions x2 + 15 theorem-like results x3 + 6 proofs x4) exceeds the Level 4 upper bound of 80 but not 2x (160). Much of the excess is Section 2's long recapitulation of known Fraenkel-Mostowski material (Gabbay-Pitts, Gabbay) rather than new results.

verdict.summary: Formal semantics paper proving equivalence of a nominal and the standard πI-calculus semantics; formalism is native to the subject but inflated by background recap, and the main proof treats only a few cases.

papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Reformulates the labelled transition semantics of the πI-calculus in nominal logic (FM set theory with the N quantifier) and proves it equivalent to Sangiorgi's semantics.
**Level:** 4 (High)
**Rationale:** An equivalence proof between two operational semantics of a process calculus is comparable to soundness and completeness results for type systems. It does not set up a verification framework or prove undecidability, so Level 5 is not justified.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 16 (2.1-2.4, 2.8, 2.14, 2.16, 2.20, 2.22, 3.1-3.5, 4.3, 4.5)
- Theorems: 15 (theorems, propositions, lemmas and corollaries 2.5, 2.6, 2.11, 2.17-2.19, 2.23, 2.24, 2.26, 2.27, 4.7-4.11)
- Proofs: 6 (2.18, 2.19, 4.8, 4.9, 4.10, 4.11)
- Equations: many (axioms, transition rules)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 101
Expected range (Level 4): 30-80
Ratio: 1.26x upper bound

**Assessment:** Elevated. In this domain set membership, permutation actions and freshness are the subject matter, so none of it is theater. But roughly half the apparatus restates known FM-set theory (the ZFA axioms, cumulative hierarchy, abstraction, support results) for self-containment, and several of the 'Examples' and 'Remarks' carry informal claims stated as if proved.

### Issues
- The main Theorem 4.11 proof says the authors 'analyze only few cases. The rest of them are analogue or trivial' and omits COM and the input cases, the most delicate ones.
- Lemma 4.7 is stated without proof. Item 6 matches rule 8 (communication) with OUT_SnI, apparently a typo for COM_SnI.
- Remark 4.12 says part of the argument 'is done only in our mind', which is an unusual standard of rigour for a paper whose whole contribution is a formal equivalence.
- The text has broken references (e.g. 'because of Proposition .' in Example 2.7(5)).

---

## Citation Analysis

24 references, 4 self-citations ([1]-[4], Alexandru and Ciobanu), SCR 16.7%. [3] (nominal semantics of mobility) and [4] (the conference version of this paper) are directly relevant. [1] (nominal groups) and [2] (nominal event structures) belong to the same nominal-techniques programme but have only marginal bearing on πI-calculus semantics (similarity about 0.4-0.5). The rest of the list is appropriate (Gabbay, Pitts, Sangiorgi, Milner, Bengtson-Parrow).

---

## Structural Analysis

The central claim rests on a proof that is only partially carried out. Related work is reasonably discussed. The only limitation-like remark is that the agreement between presentations 'may break down for more powerful systems', a weak inline acknowledgment. Nothing to release (pure theory). The paper is an extended journal version of [4].

---

## Conclusion

A legitimate formal-semantics contribution whose notation is appropriate to its subject. Its weaknesses are a heavy background recap that inflates the formal apparatus, and an equivalence proof that skips the cases most likely to fail. The result is plausible, but the paper does not fully demonstrate it.

paper.title: A Secure Image Based Watermarking for 3D Polygon Mesh
paper.abstract: Proposes a non-blind spatial-domain watermarking scheme for 3D polygon meshes. Vertices are grouped by mean curvature (deep regions) and by a mantissa bit of the vertex normal; a hash of a secret image selects which vertices are displaced radially. Robustness to smoothing, subdivision, simplification and RST attacks and visual quality (Hausdorff, RMS, mean observation score) are evaluated on six models.

artifact_assessment.evidence: "The Author would like to thank Stanford 3D Scanning Repository for providing 3D Model" (Armadillo, Bunny, Dragon are public Stanford models); no code link.

flag_details.FORMALISM_THEATER: Level 2 heuristic watermarking paper that introduces the mesh as G = (V, F) with set-builder definitions of the vertex, face and edge sets. These are never used in any derivation or algorithm step and add nothing a programmer reading an .obj file would need.
flag_details.UNNECESSARY_SET_THEORY: V = {V_i in R^3 | 1 <= i <= N}, F = {F_j | 1 <= j <= M} and E = {{i,j} | i,j in I, ...} are set notation for the vertex, face and edge arrays of a mesh file; the notation never appears again.

verdict.summary: Applied 3D-mesh watermarking heuristic with decorative set notation for the mesh arrays, a factual error about MD5, an unsubstantiated 'secure' claim and only qualitative comparison with prior work.

papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Spatial-domain, non-blind watermarking of triangle meshes by radially displacing vertices chosen by curvature class and a hash-derived bit mask.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** Combines existing tools (mean-curvature estimation from Meyer et al., MD5, spherical coordinates, Hausdorff and RMS metrics) into a heuristic embedding rule. No new algorithmic analysis.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: about 3 inline (mesh G=(V,F), vertex set, face set, edge set)
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 12 (spherical coordinate conversion, Hausdorff, RMS, MoS, scaling)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 6
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0.4x upper bound

**Assessment:** Within the count range, but the Necessity Test fails for the set-theoretic mesh definitions (Section 3.2). They are never referenced again; the algorithm is described entirely in prose and pseudocode. The coordinate and metric equations are standard and acceptable.

### Issues
- 'V= {Vi in R3 | 1 <= i <= N} ... E={{i,j}|i,j in I,{i,j}} is an edge}' is set notation for arrays, and the edge definition is circular as printed.
- The paper says MD5 'produces 32 words of 8 bits i.e. 256 bit hash code', but MD5 produces 128 bits (and 32x8 = 256 is itself inconsistent with MD5's 16 bytes). The whole selection scheme is built on 256 bits.
- The bin-construction step ('create ten bins of S1 ... move vertices ... greater than m/2') is ambiguous, and Algorithm 1 uses the 5th mantissa bit where the text says the nth.
- 'Correlation' is called 'equivalent to Bit Error Rate' but then defined as the fraction correctly detected, i.e. the complement of BER.

---

## Citation Analysis

24 references, no self-citations (SCR 0%). The references are relevant to mesh watermarking and quality assessment.

---

## Structural Analysis

The experimental tables support robustness numbers for six models. The claim to be 'secure' rests only on the secret image and strength being kept as keys; there is no security analysis. The comparison with Cho et al. [10] is asserted ('produces staircase like distortion', 'less RMS error') with no figures or numbers. The subjective MoS study gives no number of observers. Weaknesses (e.g. the Cow model's sensitivity to smoothing) are noted inline, but there is no limitations section. The test meshes are public Stanford scans, which counts as public data. No code is released.

---

## Conclusion

A routine applied watermarking paper. Its decorative set-theoretic description of the mesh triggers the zero-tolerance formalism rule at Level 2. Beyond that, a basic factual error about MD5's output length, an unsupported security claim and a non-quantified comparison with the main baseline weaken the evidence.

paper.title: Sequential Algorithms for Constructing an "Out-of-Place" Multidimensional Quad-Tree Index for Answering Exact and Approximate Fixed-Radius Nearest Neighbor Queries
paper.abstract: Presents top-down and bottom-up sequential algorithms for building a multidimensional quad-tree index in which objects are also associated with nodes they do not intersect, so that a fixed-radius nearest neighbour query (exact up to Rmin, approximate up to Rmax) needs to search only one node. Continues the authors' earlier in-place indexing work.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

verdict.summary: Algorithm-design paper with pseudocode and a case-based constant-factor approximation argument; formalism is light and appropriate, but there is no implementation, experiment or complexity analysis to back the efficiency motivation.

papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Construction of an 'out-of-place' quad-tree index (objects replicated to neighbouring nodes) supporting exact and approximate fixed-radius nearest-neighbour queries with a single-node search.
**Level:** 3 (Medium)
**Rationale:** Proposes new indexing algorithms and argues a constant-factor approximation guarantee for the approximate requirement, which places it at the novel-algorithm level. The proof is informal and builds on the authors' prior framework, so nothing higher is warranted.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 numbered (helper functions defined in prose)
- Theorems: 0 numbered
- Proofs: 1 (Section 9, constant-factor approximation by cases)
- Equations: few; 8 pseudocode algorithms

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 4
Expected range (Level 3): 10-40
Ratio: 0.1x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate, arguably light. Set notation inside the pseudocode (NDN union {Q}, ExtNeighbors(A) intersected with NDN) describes genuine set operations on node-id collections at Level 3 and is acceptable.

### Issues
- The Section 9 argument is a sketch. Several bounds are stated as 'it is easy to prove' or 'should be obvious', and the constant is never given explicitly for the optimised version. One ratio is garbled in the text ('O1F rac').
- Algorithm 2 adds Q rather than Q' to NDN inside the loop over Q', which appears to be a bug.
- The paper repeatedly says it addresses efficiency, and the conclusion says the methods 'can speed up' queries, but there is no time or space complexity analysis beyond 'depends on MaxLevel and object sizes', and no experiments.

---

## Citation Analysis

22 references, 2 self-citations ([20] Andreica and Tîrşa, [21] Andreica and Ţăpuş), SCR 9%. [21] is the direct predecessor and is essential. [20] (line-constrained geometric server placement, published in Metalurgia International) is cited for lower-envelope algorithms. It is topically adjacent computational geometry, but the venue is unrelated to the subject (similarity about 0.5). No other concern.

---

## Structural Analysis

The claims are design claims supported by pseudocode and a sketched proof. Practical benefit is asserted, never measured. Limitations are acknowledged inline: no parallel 'out-of-place' method, unexplored intermediate schemes, and failure to reach a top-down constant-factor approximation. No implementation is released, although an indexing algorithm would naturally have one.

---

## Conclusion

A reasonable algorithmic extension of the authors' earlier work. Its formalism is restrained and appropriate. The evidence is thin: no implementation, no experiment and no explicit complexity bounds, so the efficiency motivation goes untested, and the approximation proof would need tightening to be convincing.

paper.title: An Improved Authentication Protocol for Session Initiation Protocol Using Smart Card and Elliptic Curve Cryptography
paper.abstract: Shows that Zhang et al.'s smart-card and ECC based authenticated key agreement protocol for SIP is vulnerable to user impersonation by a malicious registered user, and proposes a modified protocol, based on He et al.'s scheme, claimed to resist this and other attacks at lower computational cost.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

flag_details.NO_LIMITATIONS: No limitations section or inline acknowledgment. The security analysis is informal, with no formal model or proof, and this is never stated as a limitation; the conclusion is truncated mid-sentence.

verdict.summary: Break-and-fix SIP authentication paper; the protocol notation is necessary, but the security analysis is informal and the proposed protocol's specification is internally inconsistent.

papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Cryptanalysis of Zhang et al.'s SIP smart-card authentication scheme (user impersonation) and a modified ECC-based protocol.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** An incremental modification of an existing protocol family (adapted from He et al. [20]), with heuristic, attack-by-attack security arguments. No security proof in a formal model is given, so it does not reach the Level 4 cryptographic-guarantee band.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: protocol message computations (about 20 inline expressions)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. The algebraic notation (points, scalars, hashes, concatenations) is the protocol itself; an implementer needs every term, so the Necessity Test passes.

### Issues
None in terms of formalism theater. The specification itself has substantive errors:
- In the proposed authentication phase the server computes K = cT = cbP, but the user's Step 3 still uses K = b h(h(PW||a)||username) S, copied from Zhang et al. That does not equal cbP, so honest parties would not agree on K. SK is defined with r on one side and without r on the other, and r is never generated.
- V is written as 'b(s + h(username)^-1 P)', which is not well formed.
- The password-change phase of the 'new' protocol is copied verbatim from Zhang et al. and recomputes R* with the old, broken formula.
- In the attack on Zhang et al., step 3 uses h(username) rather than h(username_i), which makes the attack description inconsistent.
- The conclusion breaks off mid-sentence ('the proposed scheme is more').

---

## Citation Analysis

21 references, no self-citations (the cited Wu L. is a different author), SCR 0%. The references cover the SIP-authentication break-and-fix chain appropriately.

---

## Structural Analysis

The cryptanalysis is plausible in outline. The security claims (resistance to seven attacks, mutual authentication, perfect forward secrecy) are each supported by a one-paragraph informal argument, with no formal model, BAN logic or reduction. Given the specification errors above, these arguments are not about a well-defined protocol. The efficiency comparison counts operations only. No limitations are stated. Nothing to release beyond the protocol description.

---

## Conclusion

The formalism is appropriate, but the paper is weak structurally. The proposed protocol is not consistently specified, the security analysis is informal, and the manuscript shows signs of insufficient proofreading (a truncated conclusion, phases copied from the attacked scheme). Its main claim, an improved and secure protocol, is not adequately established.

paper.title: OPINCAA: A Light-Weight and Flexible Programming Environment For Parallel SIMD Accelerators

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Engineering description of a C++ embedded DSL (operator overloading) and toolchain for programming a custom FPGA SIMD accelerator, with simulator and profiling tools.
**Level:** 1 (Trivial)
**Rationale:** A software-environment and system-architecture description that combines established techniques (operator-overloading code generation, pipe-based DMA drivers, kernel caching, brute-force tuning). No new algorithm or model.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 0 (code listings only)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 0
Expected range (Level 1): 0-5
Ratio: 0x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. The system is described in prose and code, as it should be.

### Issues
None identified.

---

## Citation Analysis

10 references, 1 self-citation ([2], the Connex-ARM accelerator paper by the same group), SCR 10%. It is directly relevant, being the hardware the environment targets. The reference list is short and partly vendor material, but there is no manipulation pattern.

---

## Structural Analysis

The evaluation covers kernel assembly speed on four machines, database-caching speedup (up to 6x on weak hosts, none or negative on fast ones), simulator speed relative to hardware, GPU-simulator slowness, and one DMA transfer-splitting example. The 'light-weight' claim is never measured (no memory footprint figures), and there is no application-level productivity or performance comparison with alternatives such as hand-written assembly or OpenCL. Some negative results are reported honestly inline (no speedup on M1; the GPU simulator is 10x slower), and future work is listed, but there is no limitations section. No code is linked, although OPINCAA is the paper's contribution. The Figure 7 caption duplicates Figure 6's.

---

## Conclusion

A clear, honest engineering description with no formalism theater. Its weaknesses are a narrow evaluation that does not test the paper's productivity or light-weight claims, and the absence of any route to obtain the tool it presents.

paper.title: Ordering Trees by Sum-Connectivity Indices
paper.abstract: Extends earlier work on the sum-connectivity index of trees by determining the n-vertex trees with the fourth to seventh largest and the fourth to eighth smallest sum-connectivity indices, each for the stated ranges of n.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

flag_details.EXCESSIVE_SELF_CITATION: 6 of 10 references include the corresponding author B. Zhou ([1], [2], [3], [8], [9], [10]), SCR 60%, far above 30%. All six concern the sum-connectivity index and are topically relevant, so this is a ratio finding, not an irrelevance finding; the reference list is essentially the author's own research line plus four classic Randić-index sources.
flag_details.ELEVATED_FORMALISM: Formalism complexity 60 (10 lemmas and 2 theorems x3 = 36, plus 6 proofs x4 = 24) exceeds the Level 3 upper bound of 40 but stays below 80. The apparatus is necessary for the case analysis; the excess reflects the length of the enumeration, not decoration.
flag_details.NO_LIMITATIONS: No conclusion, discussion or limitations; the paper ends with the final proof.

verdict.summary: Technically careful extremal enumeration of trees by sum-connectivity index, with necessary but extensive formalism; the reference list is dominated by the corresponding author's own work (60% self-citation).

papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Ordering n-vertex trees by the sum-connectivity index, extending the known first-three extremal trees to the fourth-seventh maximum and fourth-eighth minimum.
**Level:** 3 (Medium)
**Rationale:** Proves new extremal ordering results through transformation lemmas and calculus-based monotonicity arguments. It is an incremental extension of [10] by direct case analysis, which keeps it at Level 3.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 numbered (pendant path, T_n(n1,n2,n3), S_{n,p} and T_{n,a} defined inline)
- Theorems: 12 (Lemmas 1-10, of which 1, 3, 7, 8, 9, 10 are quoted from prior work; Theorems 1-2)
- Proofs: 6 (Lemmas 2, 4, 5, 6; Theorems 1, 2)
- Equations: extensive inequality chains

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 60
Expected range (Level 3): 10-40
Ratio: 1.5x upper bound

**Assessment:** Elevated by count but substantively necessary. Every lemma feeds the two theorems, and the numerical comparisons cannot be expressed informally.

### Issues
- There are several typesetting errors in conditions: 'n1 + n2 + n3 − 5' should read '= n − 5', and 'Case 2. p − 2' should read 'p = n − 2'.
- Theorem 2(i)-(ii) cover n = 6, 7, while the proof's ψ(n) identity holds only for n >= 7, so the small cases are not explicitly verified.
- In Theorem 2's proof, the step 'by Lemma 8, χ(T_{n,n−5}) < χ(T_n(n−6,0,1))' appears to cite the wrong lemma.

---

## Citation Analysis

10 references; B. Zhou is a co-author of [1], [2], [3], [8], [9], [10], so SCR is 60%. The cited works are all on the sum-connectivity index and are genuinely used (Lemmas 1, 3, 7, 9 and 10 come from [10]; Lemma 8 from [1]), so topical similarity is high and IRRELEVANT_SELF_CITATION does not apply. The excessive-ratio condition is nevertheless met unambiguously. There is no engagement with work on the index by other groups beyond the original Randić sources.

---

## Structural Analysis

The claims are theorems supported by proofs, and the case analysis is mostly complete. The paper has no introduction to open problems, no conclusion and no limitations. Nothing to release (pure theory).

---

## Conclusion

The mathematics is competent, if incremental, and its formalism is necessary even though it exceeds the Level 3 band by count. The disqualifying issue is citation conduct: six of ten references are the corresponding author's own, which by the framework's rules caps the paper regardless of the quality of the proofs.

paper.title: A Note on the Reversibility Of Elementary Cellular Automaton 150 With Periodic Boundary Conditions
paper.abstract: Revisits the known reversibility result for elementary cellular automaton rule 150 with periodic boundary conditions and gives the inverse automaton explicitly as a circulant transition matrix (rather than a transition dipolynomial), claiming a more efficient way to compute the inverse evolution.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text

flag_details.NO_LIMITATIONS: No limitations or discussion of scope; the three-sentence conclusion only restates the claimed efficiency gain.

verdict.summary: Short note giving a circulant-matrix form of the inverse of ECA 150; the formalism is necessary, but the headline efficiency claim is weakly supported and the transition matrix is misprinted.

papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Explicit inverse of the linear elementary cellular automaton rule 150 (periodic boundary) via circulant matrices over F2.
**Level:** 3 (Medium)
**Rationale:** Proves a new closed form (Theorem 3) for an inverse already known to exist, using elementary circulant-matrix arguments. The result is a modest mathematical property, at the low end of Level 3.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 0 numbered (ECA, global transition function, reversibility given inline)
- Theorems: 4 (Proposition 1 and Theorem 2 cited from [7]; Theorem 3; Corollary 4)
- Proofs: 1 (Theorem 3, case n ≡ 2 mod 3 left as 'similar')
- Equations: about 26

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 16
Expected range (Level 3): 10-40
Ratio: 0.4x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate. The matrices and the theorem are the content; the Necessity Test passes.

### Issues
- Equation (7) prints M_n with zeros on the diagonal (first row 0 1 0 ... 0 1), which is the matrix of rule 90, not rule 150. The proof itself uses a first column (1,1,0,...,0,1), consistent with rule 150, so the displayed matrix is wrong.
- Equation (8) mixes the variables x and y in D(x).
- The efficiency claim compares O(n log n + n log n log log n) for dipolynomial multiplication with O(n log n) for a circulant matrix-vector product. Multiplying by a circulant matrix is the same operation as cyclic polynomial multiplication, so the claimed gain is an artefact of quoting bounds from different sources. Both representations encode the same object, and no runtime measurement is given.
- Only the n ≡ 1 (mod 3) case is proved, and only Q·M_n (M_n·Q is 'similar').

---

## Citation Analysis

11 references, 1 self-citation ([7], Hernández Encinas and del Rey, the dipolynomial solution this note revisits), SCR 9%. Directly relevant.

---

## Structural Analysis

The main mathematical claim is supported by a partial proof. The 'more efficient and effective algorithm' claim in the abstract and conclusion rests on a single asymptotic comparison that does not withstand scrutiny, with no experiment. No limitations are stated. Nothing to release (theory note).

---

## Conclusion

A brief, correct-in-substance note whose formalism matches its subject. Its selling point, efficiency over the dipolynomial approach, is not convincingly established, and a misprinted transition matrix plus partially omitted proof cases reduce its reliability as a reference.

paper.title: Distributed Scheduling on Utility Grids
paper.abstract: Proposes two online broker scheduling heuristics for parallel applications on utility grids, EMCT and EMET, which combine MCT and MET with TOPSIS multi-criteria ranking over time, cost and a new processing-element (PE) weight. Evaluated in GridSim with Lublin and DAS-2 workload models in terms of user satisfaction and application failures.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text (simulation uses the third-party GridSim toolkit and synthetic jobs drawn from published workload models)

flag_details.FORMALISM_THEATER: Level 2 application of TOPSIS to broker scheduling that defines applications, resources and time slots as formal tuples (a_i = (al_i, ap_i, ad_i, as_i, aη_i, aδ_i), r_i = (rc_j, rs_j, rp_j, rb_j, rt_j), ts_k = (ts_k, tf_k, tp_k)) and enumerated sets (R = {r_j, ..., r_m}, TS, A), with Greek letters for user weights. These are plain record fields and lists, already restated in Table 1, and add nothing beyond the pseudocode.

verdict.summary: Straightforward TOPSIS-based grid scheduling heuristics with decorative tuple and set notation for plain records; the evaluation compares only the two proposed variants despite claiming superiority over existing approaches.

papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Online cost/time-aware selection of grid resources for rigid parallel jobs by ranking candidate time slots with TOPSIS.
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** Applies an existing multi-criteria method (TOPSIS) on top of existing heuristics (MCT, MET) in a standard simulator. It is a straightforward application, not a new algorithm with analysis.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: about 3 inline tuple definitions (application, resource, time slot), plus enumerated sets R, TS, A
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 12 (execution, response, cost and transfer time; standard TOPSIS steps; user-satisfaction metric)

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 6
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0.4x upper bound

**Assessment:** Within range by count, but the tuple and set formalisation of records fails the Necessity Test (a struct with six fields). The TOPSIS equations are standard and acceptable.

### Issues
- 'Each application is characterized by ai = (ali, api, adi, asi, aηi, aδi)' and 'R = {rj, rj+1 ..., rm}' are notation for a record and a list, duplicated by Table 1.
- The TOPSIS equations as printed are garbled: A+ is defined with max although the text says the positive ideal is the minimum for this minimisation problem; eq. (11) reads '= 0 <= c <= 1'; and Step 7 returns the resource with minimum closeness, which contradicts standard TOPSIS.
- 'The objective is to minimize the user benefit because less user satisfaction is better' inverts the meaning of the paper's own metric, which makes the results hard to read.

---

## Citation Analysis

28 references, 1 self-citation ([10], Bansal and Hota on refinery scheduling heuristics), SCR 3.6%. Relevant (task scheduling). No issues.

---

## Structural Analysis

The abstract claims the algorithms 'perform better over existing approaches', and the conclusion that they 'lead to more efficient resource allocation than other optimal resource allocation approaches'. The experiments, however, compare only EMCT against EMET; no baseline from the related work (e.g. Garg et al.'s MinCTT, or Buyya's cost/time optimisation) is evaluated. The complexity and memory advantages claimed in the abstract are never measured. The figure-level observations are supported by plots averaged over ten trials, with no variance reported. Limitations are acknowledged inline (dependent jobs not addressed; Globus deployment as future work). No code or configuration is released; GridSim and the workload models are third-party.

---

## Conclusion

A routine application of TOPSIS to grid brokering. Decorative tuple and set notation for plain records triggers the zero-tolerance rule at Level 2. More substantively, its central comparative claim against existing approaches is not tested, and the printed TOPSIS formulation contains errors.
